title: The banyan in the seed
hook: Uddalaka has his son break open a banyan seed, and Samkhya argues the effect is already in its cause
carry: the effect already lives in its cause
tomorrow: Why would the seer and the world ever meet?

segments.voice: Yesterday the Samkhya Karika reasoned its way to the witness: a bed is made for a sleeper outside it. Today, the Karika on cause and effect, and a much older story about a seed.
screen: `A BED FOR SOMEONE.` · `A SEED, BROKEN OPEN.`

segments.voice: In the Chandogya Upanishad, a young man named Shvetaketu comes home after twelve years of study, quite pleased with himself. His father, Uddalaka, asks him one question his teachers never covered, and the son can't answer it. So the father teaches him at home. Bring me a fruit from that banyan tree, he says. Break it. What do you see? Tiny seeds, sir. Break one of those. What do you see now? Nothing at all, sir.
screen: `TWELVE YEARS OF STUDY.` → `BREAK THE SEED.` → `NOTHING AT ALL, SIR.`

segments.voice: And the father says, in paraphrase: that fine essence you can't see, my son, is what this whole great banyan stands on. The tree was already in the seed. Earlier in the same lesson he asks a sharper question: how could something that is come from what is not? Centuries later the Samkhya Karika turned that kind of intuition into an argument, and named it in one verse: sat karyam, the effect already is. That's satkarya. Its reasons: nothing comes from what doesn't exist at all; you need the right material; not everything comes from everything. Commentators give an example still used in classrooms: press sesame and you get oil, press sand all day and you get none. The old teachers also point to milk becoming curd, and Nani's kitchen still shows it: a spoon of yesterday's curd in warm milk, one quiet night, and by morning, dahi. Nobody built it. It unfolded. So for Samkhya, creation isn't something out of nothing. The whole world was folded inside prakriti, the root, and it unfolds. Not every Hindu school agrees. Nyaya and Vaisheshika argue a pot is a genuinely new thing, and the tradition keeps both arguments in the room. Uddalaka takes the seed somewhere Samkhya won't follow: that fine essence, he says, is the self of the whole world, and you are that. Many teachers draw one lesson from both: what you will become isn't bolted on from outside. It's already in you, waiting for its conditions.
screen: `THE TREE WAS IN THE SEED.` · `SAT KARYAM: THE EFFECT ALREADY IS.` · `SESAME GIVES OIL. SAND DOESN'T.` · `NYAYA SAYS: THE POT IS NEW.` · `YOU ARE THAT.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and picture the banyan seed, broken open, nothing to see inside. Bring to mind one beginning in your life right now, a friendship, a habit, a hope, and look at it the way Uddalaka looked at the seed: the whole tree already folded in. With each out-breath, let it rest there. If you pray, you can hold that beginning in prayer.
The Samkhya Karika. Its argument on causes: the effect already exists in its cause, so the world unfolds from prakriti instead of appearing from nothing.
Your line: the effect already lives in its cause. The banyan was in the seed. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1177 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHY WOULD THE SEER AND THE WORLD EVER MEET?`

howItsDone: Students of Indian philosophy learn the debate over causation, Samkhya's view that the effect pre-exists in its cause against the Nyaya-Vaisheshika view that it is newly made, and the Chandogya's banyan seed is told in homes and classrooms as a picture of the unseen essence.

chat.meaning: Samkhya's satkarya: the effect already exists in its cause, and not everything comes from everything. Uddalaka showed his son a banyan seed with nothing visible inside, the whole tree hidden in it.

satkarya.meaning: the view that the effect already exists in its cause

prakriti.meaning: the root everything seen unfolds from, thoughts included

Nyaya.meaning: the school of logic, which holds the pot is new

Vaisheshika.meaning: the school of atoms, Nyaya's close neighbor

Uddalaka.meaning: the father who teaches his son with a banyan seed in the Chandogya

tat tvam asi.meaning: you are that: Uddalaka's words to his son

notes: Karika 9 paraphrased as five reasons (asad-akaranat, upadana-grahanat, sarva-sambhava-abhavat, shaktasya shakya-karanat, karana-bhavat) without stating the count. Confirm the glosses.
Sesame-oil-not-sand example attributed to 'commentators' (it appears in Gaudapada's and later commentaries). Confirm. The yogurt hook is the writer's own illustration, not from the text.
'Satkarya' presented as a name later thinkers used for the view; confirm phrasing (satkaryavada).
Nyaya-Vaisheshika asatkaryavada (arambhavada) presented as the other side without ranking. Confirm.
The world folding back into prakriti (pralaya) is stated briefly; confirm it fits classical Samkhya.
